cues.text: From Pharmacist to Priest
Born in 1541 at Diecimo, near Lucca in Tuscany, John trained as a pharmacist's assistant in his youth.
He became a certified apothecary, a trade that gave him direct daily contact with Lucca's sick and poor.
Eventually, this work drew him toward a religious vocation.
He was ordained a priest around 1572.
Gathering Laymen for Charity

As a young priest, John gathered a group of devout laymen to work alongside him in the city's hospitals and prisons, becoming deeply engaged with the reforming spirit of the recently concluded Council of Trent .
Convinced the Church needed a new kind of religious community dedicated specifically to catechesis, preaching, and pastoral renewal, he proposed founding just such a congregation.
Founding Amid Fierce Opposition

John's proposal met with intense resistance from both Protestant sympathizers and civic leaders of the Republic of Lucca, who suspected the new community of harboring political as well as religious ambitions.

Despite this opposition, in 1574 he founded his congregation at the church of the Madonna della Rosa in Lucca; formal episcopal approval came only in 1583, with papal confirmation by Clement VIII following in 1595.
A Life in Exile from Home
The persecution John faced from Lucca's civic authorities proved so lasting that he spent much of the remainder of his life effectively banished from his own home city.

He was only occasionally readmitted by special and reluctant permission of the Senate, extracted under papal pressure—a painful irony for a man whose whole mission had been the spiritual renewal of that same community.
Founding the Missionary College
Working from Rome, John established the convent of Santa Maria in Portico (later Campitelli) in 1601.
John also became a key co-founder, alongside Cardinal Jerome Vives, of a seminary dedicated to training missionaries for foreign lands.
The project helped lay the groundwork for what would become, over a decade later, the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith ( Propaganda Fide ), founded formally in 1622.
Legacy
John's congregation was formally elevated to a religious order with solemn vows in 1621 by Pope Gregory XV, taking the definitive name Clerics Regular of the Mother of God.
John himself died in Rome in 1609, worn out after nursing his own brethren through an outbreak of influenza.

Canonized in 1938, he is remembered both as a determined reformer who endured lasting exile from his own community, and as a quiet architect of the Church's later, more organized approach to worldwide missionary formation.
